items.source:
Abstract
Long-context models lose recall on distant evidence. We propose Sparse Attention Routing (SAR), which routes tokens to a small set of memory slots.
Methods
SAR replaces the dense attention of every fourth transformer layer. We train on 38 billion tokens for 3 epochs.
Results
On the benchmark test split SAR reaches 87.4 percent exact-match accuracy, compared with 79.1 percent for the dense baseline. Removing the moving-average update reduces accuracy to 83.0 percent. SAR did not improve results on short questions.
Discussion
The gains may concentrate on questions whose evidence lies more than 64k tokens from the question.
Limitations
We evaluated only English text and a single model scale of 7 billion parameters.

claims.label: SUPPORTED

items.source:
Abstract
We study a lightweight pruning method, Gradual Width Pruning (GWP), for convolutional image classifiers. GWP removes channels during training instead of after it.
Methods
We prune 10 percent of the channels every 5 epochs until 50 percent remain. All models use a ResNet-18 backbone and are trained for 90 epochs.
Results
On the held-out test set the pruned network keeps 69.2 percent top-1 accuracy, against 70.1 percent for the unpruned network. Inference latency falls from 41 ms to 27 ms on a single CPU core. Pruning after training lowers accuracy to 66.8 percent.
Discussion
The latency gain was measured on one CPU and may not carry over to GPUs.
Limitations
We tested a single backbone and a single dataset. We did not study robustness to distribution shift.

claims.text: GWP removes channels during training instead of after training.
claims.label: SUPPORTED

claims.text: The pruned network keeps 69.2 percent top-1 accuracy, against 70.1 percent unpruned.
claims.label: SUPPORTED

claims.label: CONTRADICTED

claims.text: GWP speeds up inference on GPUs as well.

Abstract
We report a cohort study of sleep duration and reaction time in 412 adult volunteers. Participants wore a wrist sensor for 14 nights.
Methods
Reaction time was measured each morning with a standard 5-minute test. Sleep duration was taken from the sensor.
Results
Each additional hour of sleep was associated with a 6 ms faster mean reaction time. The association was weaker in participants over 60. Caffeine intake was not related to reaction time in this sample.
Discussion
These results suggest, but do not establish, that longer sleep improves alertness.
Limitations
Volunteers were not randomly selected, and sensor-based sleep estimates were not checked against laboratory measures.
